ca_kindercare_boulders.blurb: A small hillside patch of boulders in the Santa Ana Mountains of Orange County, split into an upper and a lower cluster. It is bouldering only, with 19 problems that lean easy: most fall between VB and V3, with a few stiffer ones climbing up to V6. That makes it a relaxed place for beginners or for a low-pressure day, and it tends to be quiet. The granite is crumbly in places, so test holds before pulling hard. A past wildfire stripped much of the brush that once hid the rocks, and volunteers have kept clearing the area since.

ca_little_baldy.blurb: A bald granite summit a little above 8,000 feet inside Sequoia National Park, beside the Generals Highway north of Lodgepole. It holds 19 climbs, mostly trad with a handful of bolted lines. The routes follow slabs and cracks and run from one to four pitches. A couple are easy scrambly lines, the bulk sit between 5.7 and 5.10, and only a couple go harder, into the 5.11 and 5.12 range. The face dries unevenly, so some slabs come into shape early while others stay wet into spring. It feels quieter than the big Sierra walls. Wear a helmet, as loose rock can be dislodged from the top.

ca_mounds.blurb: A compact cluster of short formations in the Echo Rock area of central Joshua Tree, sitting in front of the south face of Little Hunk. The 19 climbs are mostly trad, with five top-rope lines and a couple of bolted routes. Grades run mainly from 5.5 to 5.9, with a few tougher ones reaching the 5.10s and one 5.11. The cracks start at desert level and are short, so it suits an easy half day or a warm-up while visiting the busier walls nearby. Deep Throat, a crack with a distinctive hole beside its base, is the best-known line here.

ca_grandma_peabody_boulder.blurb: The smaller of the two giant blocks that stand side by side at the east end of the Buttermilks above Bishop, right next to Grandpa Peabody. Of its 19 climbs, 17 are boulder problems and two are trad lines up its arete corners. Difficulty is wide: a few easy and moderate problems, a solid middle in V4 to V8, and some of the hardest problems in the Buttermilks above V10. The northwest face is steep and powerful, and the back side is covered in big huecos and jugs. The boulder is a short walk uphill from the parking lot, and the Southwest Arete is a tall, committing highball.
ca_grandma_peabody_boulder.parking_note: Leave the car at the Peabody Parking Area along Buttermilk Road, roughly three and a half miles in; the boulders stand right beside the lot.
ca_grandma_peabody_boulder.approach: A short walk straight up from the parking lot; the two big Peabody blocks are the first boulders you reach.

ca_west_face_7.blurb: The sunny side of Castle Rock, a limestone slab of about 150 feet in the hills near Burnt Ranch in northwest California. The 19 routes are mostly bolted sport lines, plus a few trad and one top rope. This is a hard-leaning wall: one route near 5.8, four around 5.10, and the majority between 5.12 and 5.13. The stone is described as very hard, and the climbing mixes slab, face, crack and arete. It is warmer and sunnier than the Trinity Aretes, secluded, and has good views from its high perch, so it suits cooler days better than midsummer.

ca_west_farthing_wall.blurb: A west-facing wall at roughly 9,400 feet in Tuolumne Meadows, up and to the right of Medlicott Dome. All 19 routes are trad, graded between 5.7 and 5.10, so it suits climbers who want moderate multi-pitch without the crowds of the big domes. The lower half has particularly good stone with knobs, small edges, flakes and shallow corners, while the upper wall is looser and less appealing. Newer lines are bolted but still want some gear. The wall gets sun from late morning onward and can be hot in midsummer, and the long walk in keeps it quiet.

ca_boulder_row.blurb: A conspicuous line of large boulders and mini crags on the hillside above Lake Ramona in north San Diego County, an easy first stop on the hike up. It holds 19 climbs, mostly short trad leads and top ropes with some bouldering mixed in. The roped climbs run from about 5.8 to the low 5.12s, with a cluster around 5.9 to 5.11, and the problems range from very easy to a couple of much harder ones. Most lines are easier to get to from above than from below. Reaching it takes a long hike of a few miles, so it feels remote for the region.

ca_cave_the_3.blurb: The steep main cave at Columns of the Giants, a formation of lava columns along Highway 108 in Stanislaus National Forest east of Dardanelle. All 19 routes are bolted sport climbs, and they are demanding: one around 5.11, most in the 5.12 range, and several at 5.13. The cave is ultra-steep, with the right side climbing underneath sheared-off columns, so expect powerful, jug-hauling moves and bring knee pads. Because it stays shaded through summer mornings and early afternoons at this elevation, it is a good hot-weather crag, and the base is only a short scramble up talus from the road.
ca_cave_the_3.parking_note: Pull off beside Highway 108 at the marked Columns of the Giants interest sign, just east of Dardanelle.
ca_cave_the_3.approach: Follow the path past the geology exhibit, then cross the loose talus slope up to the obvious cave. It takes only a few minutes.

_conflicts.ca_cave_the_3: Stored rock is andesite; https://www.mountainproject.com/area/107040562/columns-of-the-giants agrees (andesite) but https://touchstoneclimbing.com/trip-report-columns-giants/ calls it basalt.
